summary: Four situations lead into confession and a sin offering: withheld testimony, unnoticed contact with an unclean carcass, unnoticed contact with human uncleanness, and a rash oath. The chapter then scales the available offering from livestock to birds to flour before turning to trespass against holy things, restitution, and wrongs committed unknowingly.
whyItMatters: The chapter joins responsibility with an accessible path to forgiveness: it names concrete failures, requires acknowledgment or repayment, and adjusts the offering to the person's means.

context.author: The chapter continues instructions presented as Yahweh's words to Moses; it does not identify the book's narrator or final compiler.
context.audience: Individual Israelites, including witnesses, people who discover ritual uncleanness or a rash oath, and anyone who misuses holy property.
context.date: The narrative setting is Israel's time at Sinai; the chapter itself does not date its composition.
context.setting: Israel's camp and the Tent of Meeting, where the priest receives offerings and sanctuary-valued restitution.
context.literaryForm: A sequence of legal cases followed by graded sacrificial procedures and rules for trespass offerings.

outline.heading: Four situations that create liability
outline.note: The cases concern testimony, ritual contact, and rash speech, including acts initially hidden from the person.

outline.heading: Confession and an offering from the flock
outline.note: Recognition leads to confession, sacrifice, and priestly atonement.

outline.heading: A bird offering when a lamb is unaffordable
outline.note: Two birds serve as a sin offering and a burnt offering under a distinct procedure.

outline.heading: A flour offering when birds are unaffordable
outline.note: Fine flour without oil or frankincense supplies a further provision for the person with fewer means.

outline.heading: Trespass involving holy things
outline.note: A ram accompanies full restitution plus an added fifth.

outline.heading: Wrongdoing not yet known
outline.note: Ignorance does not remove liability, but the same sequence ends with atonement and forgiveness.

keyVerses.text: It shall be, when he is guilty of one of these, he shall confess that in which he has sinned;
keyVerses.why: Recognition of a named failure leads first to confession before the required offering is brought.

keyVerses.text: “‘If he can’t afford a lamb, then he shall bring his trespass offering for that in which he has sinned, two turtledoves, or two young pigeons, to Yahweh; one for a sin offering, and the other for a burnt offering.
keyVerses.why: The first alternative explicitly adjusts the required offering when a lamb is beyond the person’s means.

keyVerses.text: He shall make restitution for that which he has done wrong regarding the holy thing, and shall add a fifth part to it, and give it to the priest; and the priest shall make atonement for him with the ram of the trespass offering, and he will be forgiven.
keyVerses.why: This verse makes repair of the loss part of addressing a trespass against sanctuary property.

keyVerses.text: “If anyone sins, doing any of the things which Yahweh has commanded not to be done, though he didn’t know it, he is still guilty, and shall bear his iniquity.
keyVerses.why: The closing case states the chapter's difficult premise that ignorance does not make a violation unreal.

questions.question: What four situations open the chapter?
questions.answer: They are failing to report known evidence after a public call to testify, unknowingly touching an unclean animal carcass, unknowingly touching human uncleanness, and making a rash oath that later becomes known. The list mixes failures of speech with ritual contact.

questions.question: Does being “unclean” mean that a person is dirty or morally corrupt?
questions.answer: No. Verses 2–3 describe ritual uncleanness after contact with specified sources, including contact a person did not notice. The passage also calls the person “guilty” when the matter becomes known and requires confession in verse 5, so the obligation is real. That wording does not make uncleanness a measure of someone’s moral worth.

questions.question: What is a public adjuration to testify?
questions.answer: It is a public demand that a witness speak about what the witness has seen or knows. Verse 1 treats withholding that knowledge after hearing the demand as a failure for which the witness bears responsibility.

questions.question: What place does confession have in the procedure?
questions.answer: Once guilt is recognized, the person is told to confess the particular failure and then bring the required offering. Confession is therefore not a substitute for the offering in this chapter; it begins the process of addressing what happened.

questions.question: How does the chapter account for different economic means?
questions.answer: A person first brings a female sheep or goat, but someone unable to afford a lamb may bring two birds. Someone unable to afford the birds may bring one tenth of an ephah of fine flour, and each path reaches priestly atonement and forgiveness.

questions.question: Why is the flour offered without oil or frankincense?
questions.answer: Verse 11 explicitly removes oil and frankincense because this is a sin offering. The chapter supplies that classification but gives no further symbolic or practical explanation for the omission.

questions.question: What makes the holy-things case a trespass offering?
questions.answer: The offense involves wrongful use of what belongs to Yahweh's holy things. The person must bring a valued ram, repay what was wrongfully used, and add one fifth, so the procedure includes both sacrifice and concrete repair of the loss.

questions.question: How can someone be guilty of something they did not know?
questions.answer: Verses 17-19 distinguish ignorance from innocence: an unknown violation is still treated as real once it is addressed. The passage does not say ignorance and deliberate defiance are identical; it provides an offering and says the priest makes atonement for the unknown act.

glossary.def: A formal public call requiring a witness to testify about what the witness has seen or knows.
A ritual status that limits approach to holy things; it is not the same as dirt or a statement of personal moral worth.
An ancient unit for measuring dry goods; this chapter requires one tenth of an ephah of flour in the lowest-cost case.
Repayment of the loss caused, here with an additional one fifth in the holy-property case.

reviewer: Codex editorial agents; independent chapter review

before.text: Chapter 4 gives sin-offering procedures for unintentional violations at different levels of Israel’s community.

here.text: Specific failures lead to confession and an offering scaled to the person’s means. The final cases require a ram and, for misuse of holy things, repayment with an added fifth.

after.text: In WEB numbering, chapter 6 begins with deception or theft against a neighbor, requiring repayment and a trespass offering, before shifting to the priests’ daily altar and offering duties.
